Preparing at home

Household production

Becker (1965) treats household time and purchased inputs as ingredients in production, giving work completed at home a place in the resource account.

Before a household reaches its tax preparer, work has already begun around the kitchen table. Receipts, statements, and records of unfamiliar transactions have to become a file someone else can understand. With AI, the household can organize those records and investigate a question before bringing in a partly completed return. Its remaining difficulty is easier to describe, even while the office uses the same software and procedures (fig. 2).

Preparing the figure

For that household, the immediate gain may be a shorter appointment or fewer hours purchased, while another conversation may reveal a question that gives a household a reason to seek advice for the first time. Following the household-production account of Becker (1965), we count preparation time alongside purchased inputs, then follow the completed file into the professional work that remains.

Keeping office tools fixed lets us compare what happens when the same preparer receives a different file for the same matter. Its contents change the hours required, the price worth paying, and the remaining work assigned to a junior colleague. We follow that colleague through the records received and the judgment learned while completing the return.

Across filing seasons

Learning through work

Arrow (1962) connects experience in production to future performance, while our diagnostic measure follows the information retained from an individual case.

Inside the office, a junior preparer may once have traced a discrepancy through supporting records and learned which distinction resolved it, linking current production to later ability through the learning-by-doing mechanism studied by Arrow (1962). When the household supplies the records, reasoning, and subsequent feedback together, the prepared file can preserve that lesson while saving work needed to complete the return.

Over successive seasons, those differences in received information enter the qualifications of people who will advise later households, while workers can also purchase instruction to acquire the judgment that their cases teach less often. Because qualification belongs to the worker and carries future earnings, study responds to the value of the remaining professional work, linking today’s customer preparation to tomorrow’s fees and available expertise.

We can follow two files that produce an equally successful return yet leave different lessons with their recipients, because one preserves the observations behind a decision while the other supplies only its conclusion. That difference becomes economically relevant when the recipient later faces another household’s problem independently and must draw on what the earlier case taught.

Prices and learning

When a novice can pay for an informative placement through a wage concession or a separate payment, the learning opportunity helps finance the service received by the household. Removing that opportunity also removes its contribution to the fee, so the private calculation already includes some of the future value of what the novice would have learned.

For the household choosing what to hand over, a file’s remaining work and learning value enter the same fee. We now examine what the prepared file teaches by following the records and feedback that reach the junior preparer after the household has finished its work.
